newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain worries about strike impact on car industry.
newsitem.headline: Spain worries about strike impact on car industry.

text.p: Spain's government voiced concern on Monday it was at risk of losing lucrative automotive contracts due to a 12-day-old truckers' strike.
Though traffic was flowing freely in most parts of Spain by Monday, many plants, especially carmakers, were forced to cut back or halt production for lack of supplies.

"It's not only a matter of targeted impact on economic growth but we are running a serious risk of losing supply contracts, especially in the automotive auxiliary sector," Industry Minister Josep Pique warned at a news conference.
The economic impact of the strike was waning with security forces ensuring free movement on the roads but concerns persisted about the risks of a prolonged disruption.

Economy Secretary in the Catalan regional government Macia Alavedra warned the strike could ruin the government's efforts to reduce inflation which is one of the key criteria for entering a European Monetary Union in 1999.
Spanish inflation for January fell below 3.0 percent for the first time in 28 years.

The conservative government has warned of steep rises in fish and produce if the strike continues. Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said at the weekend the administration would take measures to prevent economic paralysis if the strike went on.
Under government orders, Civil Guards have escorted more than 1,000 drivers in the past day for fear of retaliation from strikers parked along the hard shoulders of some main roads in northern Spain.
Meanwhile, no progress was evident in government negotiations with the organisation leading the strike, Fedatrans. The talks resumed on Monday after long but fruitless meetings at the weekend.
"For the moment, we are not moving closer on any point. We are going to see if we can unblock it," strikers' spokesman Jose Soldevilla said of the negotiations.
The key sticking point is the truckers' demand for lowering the retirement age to 60 from 65 with 100 percent of pensions.

Taxi drivers, who want the same improvement in labour conditions and lower fuel prices which the strikers are demanding also halted work for several hours on Monday and staged demonstrations across the country.
The Agriculture Ministry said markets which had been emptied of food at the end of last week were full again.
But the disruptions in supply lines last week and the reduced number of trucks on the roads due to the strike were still taking a painful toll on carmakers and the fresh foods sector in particular.
German car production was slowly grinding to a halt as critical deliveries of parts were disupted by the strike.
Volkswagen, the largest car maker in Europe, said it would suspend output of its Polo vehicle as of Tuesday in German and as of Wednesday in Paloma, Spain for lack of parts.
Opel also interrupted production at its plant in Ruesselsheim, Germany.
German car companies in Spain were also hit.
Mercedes-Benz said it had been forced to suspend production at both of its Spanish plants.
Other carmakers also felt the pinch.
Citroen, Nissan and VW subsidiary Seat in Spain cut back or halted production.
In Portugal, Ford-Volkswagen AutoEuropa cut output due to the strike.
Some factories resorted to flying in parts by plane and helicopter.
